title: Guru Amar Das: equality
hookLine: the third Guru's light: first the row, then the audience
tomorrow: what did the fourth Guru dig, and why sit beside it?

lines: FIRST THE ROW, THEN THE AUDIENCE.
cards: A seating chart is a family argument with a spreadsheet. Harjit has made one for Simran's graduation party: a head table up front for the uncles and his business partner, folding tables in back for everyone else.
Simran stares at it and sends you a screenshot. She already knows where the emperor had to sit.
Tradition says that when the emperor Akbar came to see Guru Amar Das at Goindwal, he was asked to eat in the langar first, on the floor, in the row, with everybody. First the row, then the audience.

teach.b: In Punjabi it's short: pehle pangat, piche sangat. First the pangat, the row where people sit on the floor and eat as equals; then the sangat, the gathering with the Guru.
The story is told about an emperor so that nobody else gets an excuse. Guru Amar Das's own words are in the Guru Granth Sahib, in Raag Bhairao, on Ang 1127 and 1128.
In paraphrase: let no one be proud of their caste.

Then a picture: the whole world is one clay, and the Potter shapes it into vessels of many kinds. Different shapes, the same clay. One to tell a friend tonight: the third Guru's case for equality is a pottery lesson.
Every bowl on the shelf came out of the same ground. Equality here isn't pretending everyone is identical. The vessels really are different, tall and short, plain and painted.
What's the same is what they're made of, so the row on the floor sets them side by side. And a seating chart? Simran doesn't tear it up.
She asks her dad if the head table could become one long table, with Baba Kartar in the middle, where everyone can reach him.
Harjit says he'll think about it.

how: In the langar, Sikhs and guests of any background sit together in rows, the pangat, on the floor or at shared tables, and are served the same food; the saying 'pehle pangat, piche sangat' is told with the story of Akbar's visit to Guru Amar Das.

o: a Mughal emperor who later turned to Sikh teaching
the Guru who wrote the Sikh morning prayer, the Japji
the third Guru, who seated everyone in one row first

games.q: the third Guru — tap the pairs.
p: the row where all eat as equals
the emperor who ate in the row first
shapes one clay into many vessels

s: in the story, the emperor got a seat of honor in the langar
tradition says he ate in the row, on the floor, like everybody.
Guru Amar Das pictures the world as one clay in many vessels
Raag Bhairao, Ang 1128: one clay, and the Potter shapes many kinds.
equality in Sikhi means everyone is the same
the vessels really differ; the clay is the same. the row sets them side by side.

games.q: your new job's break room: managers at the window table, the warehouse crew by the vending machines. you're new. where does pehle pangat point you?
o: the window table; equality means you're free to sit with the bosses.
wherever there's room, beside whoever's there, crew or managers.
propose a rule that everyone switches tables every week.
games.why: the row doesn't sort by rank. you sit where there's room, beside whoever is there. no one's place is above another's.

practice: Bring to mind one table you'll eat at this week: school, work or home. Name one person there you've never really sat beside, and what keeps you apart: a habit, a group, plain shyness.
Choose the moment you'll take the seat next to them, and rehearse the first thing you'll say.

wordCard.voice: Guru Amar Das: the third Guru, who put the row before the audience. One clay, many vessels, side by side.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: pangat, the row of people seated to eat as equals in the langar.

carryVoice: A line to hold: equality, everyone in the row first, the emperor included. One clay, one long table.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1127-1128 (Raag Bhairao, Mahalla 3: 'jaat kaa garab na kareeahu koee'; 'maatee ek sagal sansaaraa, bahu bidh bhaande ghadai kumhaaraa'), paraphrased
Sikh tradition: Akbar's visit to Guru Amar Das at Goindwal; 'pehle pangat, piche sangat'
